Caregiver psychoeducation meta-analysis finds moderate burden reduction

Across 12 randomized trials, psychoeducational programs combining structured dementia education with skills training reduced informal-caregiver burden versus controls by Hedges' g −0.45 (95% CI −0.61 to −0.28; p<0.001), although the abstract does not report absolute Zarit-score changes, heterogeneity or evidence certainty.

Key quantitative results: Twelve randomized trials were included and meta-analyzed. Psychoeducational interventions reduced caregiver burden versus control conditions with Hedges' g −0.45 (95% CI −0.61 to −0.28; p<0.001).

ManagementCaregiver support

Added September 30, 2026 · DOI:10.1177/07334648261490430; PMID:42811273

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The pooled estimate supports caregiver psychoeducation that pairs disease information with practical skills rather than education alone. The standardized effect is moderate and statistically precise, but the public abstract does not provide total participants, absolute Zarit-score change, intervention intensity, follow-up duration, heterogeneity, risk-of-bias summary or certainty rating. It informs service design but is not a guideline-level mandate.

Study design

The authors conducted a PRISMA 2020 systematic review and REML random-effects meta-analysis of 12 randomized controlled trials. Eligible interventions combined structured dementia education with skills-based training for informal caregivers. Caregiver burden measured by the Zarit Burden Interview or validated adaptations was the primary outcome; comparator type, mean caregiver age and gender composition were examined as moderators.

Key quantitative results

  • Twelve randomized trials were included and meta-analyzed. Psychoeducational interventions reduced caregiver burden versus control conditions with Hedges' g −0.45 (95% CI −0.61 to −0.28; p<0.001).
  • Comparator type was associated with differences in effect estimates, but the authors cautioned that subgroup analyses were exploratory and some categories contained few studies.
  • Mean caregiver age and gender composition were not significant moderators. The abstract did not report an absolute Zarit-score difference, total sample size, heterogeneity statistic or formal certainty-of-evidence rating.

What changed

A September 29 quantitative synthesis consolidates randomized-trial evidence for psychoeducational caregiver programs and estimates a moderate standardized reduction in burden.

Strength of evidence

Moderate pooled randomized evidence for reduced caregiver burden, tempered by incomplete public reporting of sample size, heterogeneity, intervention components, follow-up, risk of bias and certainty. The comparator moderator is exploratory and some subgroups were sparse.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

Programs that combine dementia education with skills training are reasonable components of caregiver support and may reduce burden. The standardized effect does not identify a universal format, dose or absolute benefit, and implementation should reflect caregiver needs, language, access and local resources.

Field medical relevance

Directly relevant to nonpharmacologic dementia management, caregiver intervention design and conversations about evidence-based supportive services beyond medication or biomarker testing.

Access or reimbursement relevance

The review supports psychoeducational caregiver services but establishes no new program availability, payer coverage or reimbursement. Local access, language, staffing and delivery format remain implementation determinants.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
What does Hedges' g −0.45 mean?
It indicates a moderate average reduction in burden on a standardized scale. The abstract does not provide an absolute Zarit-score change, so it cannot be translated directly into points for an individual caregiver.
Is this a clinical practice guideline?
No. It is a systematic review and meta-analysis of trials. It summarizes evidence but does not issue graded recommendations from a guideline body.
Which program should services adopt?
The pooled abstract does not establish one optimal format or dose. Programs should include both structured education and skills training, while selection should account for setting, caregiver needs and feasibility.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Public abstract does not report total participants or absolute Zarit-score changes
  • Intervention content, intensity and follow-up likely varied across trials
  • Heterogeneity and risk-of-bias results are not reported in the abstract
  • No formal certainty-of-evidence rating is reported publicly in the abstract
  • Comparator-type moderator analyses were exploratory with sparse categories
  • A standardized pooled effect does not identify the most effective delivery model
